edits.stem:
A 69-year-old man has had 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. A chest X-ray confirms right lower lobe consolidation. He is alert and orientated, with a temperature of 38.9°C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% on air. His C-reactive protein is markedly raised. The admitting doctor calculates his CURB65 score.

Which of his findings contributes a point to the score?

options.A: His age of 69 years on presentation

edits.correct_answer: A. His age of 69 years on presentation
edits.why_correct: CURB65 gives one point each for new confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate of 30 or more, low blood pressure (systolic under 90 or diastolic 60 or less) and age 65 or over. This man is alert, with a respiratory rate of 22 and normal blood pressure, so of the findings given only his age scores; his urea is not yet known. Fever, tachycardia, pleuritic pain and CRP are not part of the score, so clinical judgement and oxygen saturation must be used alongside it. Source: NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management, 2025 (Box 2, CURB65).

edits.stem:
A 68-year-old man who stopped smoking a few years ago has had a persistent cough and weight loss for three months. A chest X-ray shows a mass at the left hilum, and he has been referred on the suspected cancer pathway (an urgent, time-limited route to specialist assessment).

On examining his chest, which finding is most directly explained by the tumour narrowing the left main bronchus?
edits.why_correct: A tumour growing in or pressing on a main bronchus narrows the lumen, so air moving through the narrowed segment makes a localised wheeze that persists and does not clear with coughing or bronchodilators. A fixed, unilateral wheeze in a smoker or ex-smoker should prompt imaging for lung cancer rather than a trial of asthma treatment. Source: standard respiratory teaching on central airway obstruction; NICE NG12 (suspected cancer, 2015, updated) recommendation 1.1.1 supports referral on the suspected cancer pathway when chest X-ray findings suggest lung cancer.

edits.why_correct: Obesity is the most important modifiable risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea, because fat deposition around the upper airway and neck narrows the pharynx and makes it collapse during sleep. Weight loss is therefore a core part of management alongside other measures. Source: NHS sleep apnoea information (obesity listed first among linked factors) and standard teaching; NICE NG202 (2021) covers diagnosis and treatment.

edits.why_correct: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the vagus and hooks under the aortic arch, so a left hilar or mediastinal tumour (or involved nodes) can compress or invade it. This causes vocal cord palsy with a weak, hoarse voice, and hoarseness in a smoker is a red flag for lung or laryngeal cancer. A chest X-ray suggesting lung cancer needs referral on the suspected cancer pathway. Source: standard anatomy teaching; NICE NG12 (2015, updated) recommendation 1.1.1 for referral when chest X-ray findings suggest lung cancer.

It typically appears many years after the exposure. The fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer. edits.why_correct: Symmetrical bilateral effusions in a patient with decompensated heart failure and no atypical features are presumed to be transudates. The best approach is to treat the underlying heart failure with diuretics and review the response. Pleural sampling is reserved for effusions that are unilateral or asymmetrical, associated with pleuritic pain or fever, or that fail to resolve with treatment. Source: standard teaching on pleural effusion in heart failure, in line with BTS pleural disease guidance.

edits.why_correct: Peak expiratory flow is the fastest flow achieved during a forced expiration that starts from full lung inflation. The patient therefore needs an upright position, a maximal breath in, a tight lip seal and a single short, forceful blast. The manoeuvre is repeated and the highest of three readings is recorded. Source: standard UK respiratory clinical teaching and respiratory service patient guidance on peak flow meters.

issues: Citation overstated: BTS 2008 replaced by BTS Clinical Statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis (Thorax 2021;76:4-20); hypercalcaemia mechanism/steroid/avoid vitamin D is standard and consistent with it.

edits.why_correct: Activated macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without normal feedback control. This increases gut calcium absorption and bone resorption, raising calcium while PTH is suppressed. Treatment is usually with oral corticosteroids, and vitamin D supplements and a high calcium intake should be avoided. Source: BTS Clinical Statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis, Thorax 2021, and standard teaching.

issues: Pearl claims '-osis' reflects dust-induced fibrosis, which is etymologically wrong; reworded. IIDB source named precisely (prescribed disease D1, which includes coal, silica and asbestos-related pneumoconiosis).

edits.pearl: Pneumoconiosis is the umbrella term for the chronic lung diseases caused by inhaling mineral dust, and silicosis, asbestosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis all fall within it.
edits.why_correct: Pneumoconiosis is the collective term for lung diseases caused by inhaling mineral dusts such as coal dust, silica and asbestos. Coal worker's pneumoconiosis typically shows small nodular opacities in the upper zones after prolonged underground exposure. Pneumoconiosis is a prescribed disease (D1) under the UK Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit scheme, so the occupational history can matter for benefits. Source: standard occupational respiratory teaching; UK Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit scheme, prescribed disease D1.

edits.why_correct: In heart failure the raised venous and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure drives protein-poor fluid across the pleural membranes faster than the lymphatics can clear it. This produces a transudate, typically bilateral and roughly symmetrical. Inflammatory, infective and malignant effusions are usually exudates and tend to be unilateral or asymmetrical. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline, Thorax 2023, and standard teaching.
